title: Complete and consistent means exactly half of all strings are generated

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Complete and consistent means exactly half of all strings are generated

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: For a multiway system serving as an axiom system, with negation any length-preserving involution on strings, the system is complete and consistent exactly when half of all possible strings of each length are eventually generated from the string representing true; more than half implies inconsistency and less than half implies incompleteness.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the criterion for whether a system is complete and consistent is simply that exactly half the possible strings of a given length are eventually generated if one starts from the string representing "true".

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Implications for Mathematics and Its Foundations” (from p. 772), pp. 796–797. Scope: multiway systems treated as axiom systems with length-preserving negation

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-39: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The intended result is a finite combinatorial equivalence that can be proved or refuted now. The wording needs additional assumptions on negation and pairwise coverage, and formal checking can expose whether they are sufficient.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Formalize the reachable set at each string length and a fixed-point-free length-preserving involutive negation. Prove completeness and consistency iff exactly one member of every negation pair is reachable; enumerate finite examples to test edge cases.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Exactly half is insufficient unless each negation pair contributes exactly one string.

An involution with fixed points invalidates the simple half-count criterion.

Reachability may be undecidable even though the equivalence is provable.

fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Under a fixed-point-free length-preserving negation, strings come in pairs, so generating more than half forces a string and its negation, and generating less than half leaves some pair untouched. That is a short combinatorial argument and can be formalized with standard tools. The criterion for this class of multiway systems is therefore settleable by proof now; computing the fraction for one irreducible rule is a different and often undecidable question.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fix a length-preserving involution as negation and prove or refute that a multiway system is complete and consistent exactly when it eventually generates half the strings of each length from the string for true. A counterexample involution, or a gap in the pairing argument, refutes the biconditional; a checked proof confirms it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
An involution with fixed points breaks the identification of exactly half with completeness plus consistency.

For a concrete rule, the eventual fraction of strings may itself be undecidable; the general implication is what the proof settles.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If the claim holds, then for every length-preserving involution 'negation' on binary strings and every set S of strings of a given length that a multiway system could eventually generate, S is complete (every string or its negation is in S) and consistent (no string together with its negation is in S) if and only if |S| is exactly half of all strings of that length; in particular more than half implies inconsistent and less than half implies incomplete.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py enumerates all 764 involutions of the 8 binary strings of length 3 against all 256 subsets, and for length 4 the complement, reversal and identity maps plus 300 seeded random involutions against all 65536 subsets, recording for each (involution, set) whether the set is complete, consistent and of size exactly half. It then enumerates all 1485 multiway systems with one or two length-non-decreasing rules (|lhs| 1-2, |rhs| = |lhs| or |lhs|+1) over {A,B}, computes the exact closure of 'A' restricted to strings of length <= 6, and evaluates the same quantities at each length 2-6 under complement and reversal negation. Runtime 2 s.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Part 1 (sets): for length n = 3, enumerate all 764 involutions of the 8 strings and all 256 subsets S; for n = 4, take 300 pseudo-random involutions of the 16 strings (numpy seed 20261031, including the complement map, reversal and the identity-on-some-strings cases) and all 65536 subsets. For each (involution, S) record complete, consistent, |S| versus half. Part 2 (multiway systems): enumerate all multiway systems over {A,B} with one or two rules lhs -> rhs, |lhs| in {1,2}, |rhs| in {|lhs|, |lhs|+1} (length-non-decreasing so that the set of generated strings of each length <= 6 stabilises and can be computed exactly), started from the string 'A' taken to represent true; for each system and each length n = 2..6 record the exactly generated set, under negation = complement and under negation = reversal. PASS (supports) if in Part 1 and Part 2 there is no counterexample to either direction of the biconditional (complete and consistent <=> exactly half) for any involution.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. REFUTES if the biconditional fails in both directions, or if either of the book's two directional arguments (more than half => inconsistent; less than half => incomplete) has a counterexample. MIXED if the three implications the book argues for (more than half => inconsistent; less than half => incomplete; hence complete and consistent => exactly half) hold without exception but the converse (exactly half => complete and consistent) has counterexamples both among arbitrary sets and among stabilised generated sets of actual multiway systems. The number of counterexamples and the role of involution fixed points are reported.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: stabilised (multiway system, length, negation) cases that generate exactly half of the strings but are not complete and consistent

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: The book (pp. 796-797) states the criterion as an equivalence ('the criterion for whether a system is complete and consistent is simply that exactly half ... are eventually generated') but argues only the two contrapositive directions. 'Negation' is taken as the book says: any operation that preserves length and gives back the original when applied twice (a length-preserving involution), including ones with fixed points (strings equal to their own negation), for which the test records separately what happens. 'Complete' = for every string, it or its negation is generated; 'consistent' = for no string are both generated (a fixed point that is generated counts as both). 'Eventually generated' is made exact by restricting to length-non-decreasing rules so that the generated set at each length is a finite closure.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Exhaustive sets and involutions on binary strings of length 3-4, and all length-non-decreasing one- and two-rule multiway systems over {A,B} with short rules, generated by analysis.py

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
The three implications the book actually argues (more than half => inconsistent; less than half => incomplete; hence complete and consistent => exactly half) hold without exception in every enumerated case, for every length-preserving involution including those with fixed points.

The converse that makes 'exactly half' a criterion (exactly half => complete and consistent) is false: it fails for 3.94 million of the enumerated (involution, set) pairs and for 80 stabilised cases among the 1485 small multiway systems, e.g. {A -> BB, BB -> AA} from A generates exactly half of the length-6 strings while being both inconsistent and incomplete. The criterion is therefore necessary but not sufficient; it becomes sufficient only if consistency (or completeness) is known independently.

For any negation with fixed points (e.g. reversal, where palindromes are their own negation) no set is complete and consistent at all (0 of 65536 sets at length 4; 0 of the 659 fixed-point involutions at length 3 admit one), so the 'exactly half' count carries no information about completeness and consistency in that case.

The multiway enumeration is restricted to length-non-decreasing rules so that 'eventually generated' is exactly computable; this restriction excludes systems whose generated sets at a given length never stabilise, but the counterexamples found are exact.
